title: What the partner sees in the CSV
prompt: A partner gets the trips as a CSV file with a header, and opens it without a schema. Write `solve(trips)` so it saves that file at the given path and returns exactly what the partner will read from it.
rules: Save `trip_id`, `pickup_at`, `passenger_count`, `fare`, `tip` and `payment_type`, in that order, as CSV with a header line at `path`, replacing any earlier copy.
Read the file back the way the partner does: with the header, and no schema or type guessing.
Return what you read: every column is text, written the way the CSV file holds it. A missing value comes back missing.
hints: `df.write.mode("overwrite").csv(path, header=True)` writes the column names on the first line.
`spark.read.csv(path, header=True)` takes the names from that line and leaves every column as text.
Look at how a timestamp is written in the file: it isn't quite the way `show()` prints it.
starter:
def solve(trips):
    path = "/tmp/taxi/partner"
    # Save the CSV at `path` and return what the partner reads from it.
    return trips
explanation: Write and read with the header and nothing else: `trips.select(...).write.mode("overwrite").csv(path, header=True)`, then `spark.read.csv(path, header=True)`. CSV has no types, so every column comes back as text, and the text is exactly what Spark wrote: `fare` keeps its two decimals, like `52.00`, and `pickup_at` is written in full ISO form with milliseconds and a `Z` for UTC, like `2026-04-07T07:05:07.000Z`. A missing passenger count is written as an empty field, which reads back as missing. This is why a CSV copy needs its schema repeated on every read, while a Parquet copy keeps its types.
